Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

This API lets you build booking systems that manage calendar time slots. Whether you're scheduling appointments, reserving meeting rooms, or controlling access to resources, the calendar booking API handles the core logic: checking availability, creating bookings, and managing conflicts.

You'll interact with the API through standard HTTP endpoints. Create bookings, retrieve schedules, update reservations, and cancel slots using REST verbs. Responses come back as JSON so you can integrate with web apps, mobile clients, or backend systems.

Most implementations need three core pieces: a resource (what gets booked), a time slot (when it's available), and a booking (who reserved it). The API enforces rules around how far in advance people can book, maximum booking duration, and which users can access certain resources. It prevents double-booking and tracks the full history of each reservation.

The guide covers authentication, the core endpoints, error handling, and common workflows. You'll learn how to check availability before creating a booking, handle rescheduling, and manage cancellations. Code examples use curl and popular languages like Python and JavaScript so you can start integrating immediately.

Each section includes the request format, response structure, and how to handle edge cases. By the end, you'll understand the API's design and be ready to build calendar features into your application.

Add a paragraph on authentication.

All requests to the calendar booking API require authentication. Use API key authentication by including your key in the Authorization header with the Bearer scheme. Create and manage keys through your account dashboard. Each key is scoped to your account and can be revoked if needed. Keep your keys private and never commit them to version control. The API will reject any request that lacks valid credentials or uses a revoked key.

output: All requests to the calendar booking API require authentication. Your API key is a secret code that proves you're allowed to use the service. Get your key from your account dashboard. When you make a request, include this key in the Authorization header using the format "Bearer [your-key]". This tells the API who you are and validates your request. Keep your key private and never share it or put it in public repositories. If someone gets your key, they can access your entire account, so treat it with the same care as a password. Revoke old keys from your dashboard if you suspect they've been compromised.
